header.scope: Won: memberships/online billing only; studio front desks still process with Global Payments, and phase two has no date.
header.incumbent: Global Payments, through the studio software
header.tag_why: The contract sat unsigned with the controller for two weeks and was signed four days after Tobi's analysis of the customer's own failed renewals; the front-desk reader integration we couldn't show live is what kept the studios with Global.

messaging_changes.change: New proof step for recurring-revenue prospects, run before the contract goes to the finance signer: take one month of the prospect's failed renewals and show which ones usually come back with a retry or an updated card. Position it as "Their file, not our average." Bring it to the controller or finance signer, not only the evaluation lead.
messaging_changes.why: The analysis of the customer's own failed renewals was the only thing that got the silent controller to speak, and he signed four days later after the paper had sat with him for two weeks.

messaging_changes.current_line: Recover failed payments automatically with smart retries.
messaging_changes.change: For subscription and membership businesses that report churn: "Win back the members who never meant to leave." Some of the churn you report is cards that failed, not people who cancelled. Smart retries recover those payments automatically.
messaging_changes.why: The evaluation started as a board-level churn problem, and failed payments only mattered once churn was split into people who cancelled and people whose card failed; the customer's phrase "members who never meant to leave" frames recovery as churn, not as a payments feature.

messaging_changes.current_line: Online and in-store on one platform; the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
messaging_changes.change: For prospects whose front desk runs inside third-party studio software: say plainly that in-store payments work through a partner integration with [partner name], and offer a demo in the prospect's own setup showing check-in and a front-desk sale on one screen, before claiming online and in-store are unified.
messaging_changes.why: The buyer translated unified commerce into "is that the readers?", asked to see our reader inside their studio software, and we couldn't show it live, which is why the front desks stayed with the incumbent.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: Stop opening with the global positioning line for prospects whose pain is churn in a mostly domestic business; open with their churn problem and the own-data failed-renewal analysis instead.
messaging_changes.why: The rep opened with the global slide and got silence.

trigger.insight: The evaluation started as a board-level churn problem, not a payments problem; failed payments only became visible once someone split churn into people who cancelled and people whose card failed. We don't know the real size of the failed-card bucket. The rep's estimate is hedged, and the actual figure sits in Maya's board deck, which nobody on our side seems to have asked for.
trigger.messaging: Frame failed-payment recovery (M10) as recovering "members who never meant to leave" in the churn number they report to the board, not as a payments feature.

decider.insight: The rep's first answer rested on Maya's own claim that it was her call. The controller, who stayed silent through two meetings, held the paper and signed it. Maya picked the vendor, but Greg controlled whether any switch happened at all, and his questions were about termination fees, not features.
decider.messaging: Build a controller-facing proof (recoverable revenue from their own data, plus exit-cost math) into every deal where a finance signer is present, rather than pitching only to the evaluation lead.

competitor.insight: According to Maya, the incumbent answered with a rate review and a front-desk terminal bundle on a longer contract. That moved the conversation from failed payments, where our proof was strongest, to readers, studio-software integration and exit cost, where we couldn't demo. Whether the longer contract was signed for the front desks is unclear, and the rep's view that Global was rattled is his own opinion, not something the customer said.
competitor.messaging: Before the incumbent's counter-meeting, get ahead of the hardware reframe: give a clear answer on readers inside their studio software and a worked termination-fee and contract-term comparison.

message.insight: What landed was an analysis of the customer's own failed renewals, not generic benchmarks of the M4/M6 kind. It was the only thing that got the silent controller to speak. The global opener (M1) fell flat with a business whose studios are in the US and a handful in Canada. "Unified commerce" (M3) didn't register as a concept: Maya translated it into hardware, which is exactly where we were weakest.
message.messaging: Open mid-market recurring-revenue deals with a recovery analysis of the prospect's own failed-payment export instead of the global positioning slide, and drop "unified commerce" as a label in favour of the concrete front-desk scenario.

decided.insight: Until the data session the rep believed we were the comparison bid. The two-week stall ended four days after Greg saw recoverable revenue in his own data, which makes the customer-specific business case the turning point. The rep told the win story without mentioning scope; that it was only memberships and online billing came out later, under questioning.
decided.messaging: Make the customer-data recovery session a standard step before the contract goes to finance, not a rescue move after it stalls.

gaps.insight: The concrete ask was one screen at the front desk: check a member in and sell a water bottle without switching systems. We could only point to a partner, whose call came a week later, and the customer has seen the partner's demo but never in their own setup. That unproven integration is why the front desks are still with Global and why phase two has no date, so M3's online-and-in-store claim did not hold for this customer.
gaps.messaging: For prospects whose front desk runs inside third-party studio software, stop leading with M3 and say plainly that in-store goes through a named partner integration, backed by a demo in the customer's own setup.

gaps.question: What exact words did they use for their problem?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep over Slack, as he offered, for Maya's and Greg's exact phrases about failed payments, churn and the front desk. The quotes above surfaced elsewhere in the interview, not in answer to this question.

gaps.question: How big was the failed-card churn bucket?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep to request the churn split from Maya's board deck so we have the customer's real figure instead of an estimate.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep (or Greg directly, if possible) what Greg needed during the two weeks the paper sat with him, and whether anything other than the spreadsheet moved him.

gaps.question: When is phase two (studios/front desk), and what exactly is the partner integration missing?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep and the partner team for the integration status in the customer's studio software and the criteria Maya needs before moving the front desks.

gaps.question: How did we answer Greg's termination-fee and contract-term questions, and did the incumbent's longer contract lock in the front desks?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep what we told Greg about exit costs and whether Maya said if Global's terminal bundle was signed.

gaps.question: When did you first feel this was won? (scope)
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep whether the customer ever committed to moving the studios, or whether phase two is our assumption.

close.rep_takeaway: Your strongest move was showing the controller his own failed renewals rather than our averages; make that the standard step before paper goes out. Also name every signer early and report scope honestly: this was a memberships-and-online win, and the front desks are still the incumbent's to lose.
